answer:
No—the published BLEU gap alone cannot isolate the architectural effect, because the papers report different beam widths and length adjustments rather than a decoding-controlled comparison. [S:173159a1bb15#53] [S:14467d21708c#44]

- **1706.03762v7.pdf, p.8:** reports beam width **4** and length penalty **α = 0.6**, with no different decoding settings stated for base versus big models: “We used beam search with a beam size of 4 and length penalty α = 0.6 [38].” The settings were selected on the development set; maximum output length was input length + 50, with early termination when possible. [S:173159a1bb15#53]
- **1705.03122v3.pdf, p.5:** reports beam width **5**: “We use a beam of width 5.” For WMT’14 English–German, it tunes the length-normalization constant on newstest2015 and divides log-likelihoods by |y|^α: “For WMT’14 English-German we tune a length normalization constant on a separate development set (newstest2015) and we nor- malize log-likelihoods by |y|α (Wu et al., 2016).” The supplied passage does not give the selected numerical α. [S:14467d21708c#44]

Both papers therefore adjust scores for length, but the evidence does not establish identical adjustment formulas or strengths, and their beam widths differ; attributing the BLEU gap solely to architecture would leave these decoding differences uncontrolled. [S:173159a1bb15#53] [S:14467d21708c#44] Moreover, “attention instead of convolution” is an incomplete description of the comparison: 1705.03122v3.pdf, p.2 explicitly says, “We also use attention in every decoder layer”. [S:14467d21708c#9]

[S:14467d21708c#44]

Original ResNet combines an identity shortcut and residual branch by element-wise addition; DenseNet concatenates the feature maps of all preceding layers within a dense block. [S:7751b7ca31f8#23] [S:d35f04009f70#12]

In **1512.03385v1.pdf, p. 3**, the ResNet identity block is defined as “y = F(x, {Wi}) + x,” and the convolutional combination is described as “The element-wise addition is performed on two feature maps, channel by channel.” [S:7751b7ca31f8#21] [S:7751b7ca31f8#23]

In **1608.06993v5.pdf, p. 3**, DenseNet specifies that “the ℓth layer receives the feature-maps of all preceding layers, x0, . . . , xℓ−1, as input”; **p. 2** states, “instead, we combine features by concatenating them.” [S:d35f04009f70#26] [S:d35f04009f70#12]

A direct architectural implication is that ResNet’s direct identity addition requires matching dimensions: **1512.03385v1.pdf, p. 4** says, “The identity shortcuts (Eqn.(1)) can be directly used when the input and output are of the same dimensions”. [S:7751b7ca31f8#27] DenseNet’s concatenation instead accumulates feature channels within the block: **1608.06993v5.pdf, p. 4** states, “Each layer adds k feature-maps of its own to this state.” [S:d35f04009f70#35] The papers’ descriptions agree on ResNet’s summation operation: **1608.06993v5.pdf, p. 3** likewise says, “the identity function and the output of Hℓare combined by summation”. [S:d35f04009f70#26]

In ViT, a learnable class token is prepended to the embedded patch sequence; its final Transformer state serves as the image representation supplied to the classification head. [S:a990b330f233#19] The head is an MLP with one hidden layer during pre-training and a single linear layer during fine-tuning. [S:a990b330f233#19]

In DeiT’s distillation-token procedure, the class branch learns the ground-truth label, while the distillation branch learns the hard label predicted by the teacher. [S:fb364c1ec635#28] At inference, each branch’s output embedding has its own linear classifier, and late fusion adds the two classifiers’ softmax outputs to make the prediction. [S:fb364c1ec635#33]
